In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the benzodiazepines in the mediation of stress and stress-induced alterations in PRL secretion.
the study of stress and its effects on the brain and peripheral organs, and the mechanisms by which stress induces changes in these organs.
the effects of stress on the brain and peripheral benzodiazapine receptors in rats.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the sex differences observed in PBR are due to a combination of factors including: (i) differences in the sensitivity to stress; (ii) the sex differences in the stress-induced changes in circulating corticosterone levels; and (iii) sex differences in the regulation of PBR by corticosterone.

the gender difference in the stress-induced changes in PBR is not due to a gender difference in the ability of the stressor to alter the number or affinity of PBR but rather a difference in the ability to express the changes in PBR in renal tissue.
there are gender differences in the regulation of PBR in rat kidney and these differences appear to be mediated by sex hormones.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
stress-induced alterations of PBR are gender dependent.
PBR in the kidney are more sensitive to stress in males than in females.
the stress-induced decrease in PRB in the kidney is attenuated in females compared to males.
The main takeaway from our work is that
gender differences exist in the stress-induced alteration of PRB and that these differences are tissue specific.
the peripheral benzodiazapine receptor (PBR) may be a useful marker for the study of gender differences in stress response.
the sex of an individual can have a significant influence on the stress response.
